summary.text: Human spaceflight is spaceflight with a crew or passengers aboard a spacecraft, often operated directly by the people on board.
It grew out of the Cold War, when Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space on 12 April 1961 and Alan Shepard became the first American on 5 May 1961.
People have been continuously present in space on the International Space Station since 2 November 2000, and only the US, Russia and China currently have such programs.

items.prompt: Between the first American flights and the Moon landings, NASA flew two-person Gemini missions. What were they for?

options.label: To match the Soviet three-person capsule on size
To build orbital experience and techniques for the Moon trip
To test the lander by practising on the Moon
To rescue cosmonauts stranded in orbit

items.explain: Gemini's objective was to support Apollo by developing American orbital spaceflight experience and techniques to be used during the Moon mission.

items.prompt: The Soviet Voskhod capsule achieved the first spacewalk, yet the program ended. Why?

options.label: It could never carry more than one person
Its spacewalk went wrong and was never repeated
The Soviets gave up racing the Americans
It could not maneuver in orbit the way Gemini could

items.explain: Voskhod did not have Gemini's capability to maneuver in orbit, and the program was terminated.

items.prompt: The USSR built the three-person Soyuz for its Moon programs but never landed anyone. What was missing?

options.label: A big enough rocket, since the N1 never came together
A capsule that could hold three people at once
Pilots willing to attempt the long trip
Any way at all to send a craft toward the Moon

items.explain: The USSR successfully developed Soyuz, but failed to develop the N1 rocket necessary for a human landing and discontinued its lunar programs in 1974.

items.prompt: Which statement correctly compares the first American in space with the first Soviet cosmonaut?

options.label: Shepard orbited Earth once while Gagarin flew a short suborbital hop
Shepard flew first, with Gagarin following a few weeks later
Shepard flew a suborbital flight and steered his craft by hand, unlike Gagarin
Both flights were suborbital and both men steered by hand

items.explain: Gagarin completed a single orbit, while Shepard flew a suborbital flight and, unlike Gagarin, manually controlled his spacecraft's attitude.

items.prompt: What gave the Cold War rivals rockets big enough to carry the first satellites?

options.label: Giant airplanes converted to climb into space
Missiles built to deliver nuclear weapons, adapted for orbit
Weather rockets first built for science
Cargo rockets built by private companies

items.explain: The US and the USSR developed intercontinental ballistic missiles for nuclear weapons, producing rockets large enough to be adapted to carry the first artificial satellites into low Earth orbit.

items.prompt: The original Shuttle idea had a piloted, winged first stage that flew itself back. What replaced it when plans were scaled back?

options.label: A reusable space tug
Four expendable boosters
One huge liquid-fuel stage on a parachute
Two reusable solid rocket boosters

items.explain: To reduce development risk, cost and time, the piloted fly-back booster was replaced with two reusable solid rocket boosters.

pack.title: From First Orbit to Moon
pack.question: How did a Cold War rivalry take people from a single orbit to the Moon?

beats.title: From First Orbit to Moon
beats.hook: Two rival nations raced to send people up, and one of them ended up walking on the Moon.

beats.prompt: Put these early firsts in order.

items.label: Yuri Gagarin becomes the first human in space
Alan Shepard becomes the first American in space
John Glenn becomes the first American in orbit
Valentina Tereshkova becomes the first woman in space

beats.explain: Gagarin flew on 12 April 1961, Shepard on 5 May 1961, Glenn on 20 February 1962, and Tereshkova on 16 June 1963.

beats.prompt: The USSR stretched its one-person Vostok capsule into the Voskhod to rival Gemini, and won the first spacewalk. What happened to the Voskhod program?
beats.explain: Voskhod lacked Gemini's ability to maneuver in orbit, so the program was terminated.

choices.label: It was terminated, because it could not maneuver in orbit like Gemini
It went on to land crews on the Moon
choices.feedback: The Soviets did chase the Moon, but with the Soyuz spacecraft, not the Voskhod.

choices.label: It beat Gemini to the first rendezvous and docking
choices.feedback: Winning the spacewalk makes this tempting, but the US Gemini flights performed the first space rendezvous and docking.

beats.prompt: Match each program to what it did.

right.label: Carried Gagarin on the first human spaceflight
Put 12 men on the Moon in six landings
Sent Alan Shepard on the first American spaceflight
Made the first space rendezvous and docking

beats.explain: Each program was a step from the first human flights toward the Moon.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which?

steps.text: The US and the Soviet Union built intercontinental ballistic missiles to deliver nuclear weapons.
Those missiles were far too small to lift anything into orbit.
So spaceflight had to be developed using different rockets entirely.
Yet the Soviet Union launched the first satellites in 1957 and 1958.

beats.explain: The missiles produced rockets large enough to be adapted to carry the first artificial satellites into low Earth orbit.

beats.idea: Missile programs gave two rival nations rockets big enough for space, and the race between them carried people from first flights to six Moon landings.

paragraphs.heading: What it means
paragraphs.text: Human spaceflight is spaceflight with a crew or passengers on board, often with the crew flying the craft themselves. Spacecraft can also be flown from stations on the ground, or run on their own with no people involved at all. People trained to fly in space are called astronauts, or cosmonauts in Russia and taikonauts in China. Non-professionals who go are called spaceflight participants or spacefarers.

paragraphs.heading: A Cold War race
paragraphs.text: The ability to send people to space first grew out of the Cold War rivalry of the United States and the Soviet Union. Both built long-range missiles to carry nuclear weapons, and those rockets were big enough to be adapted for launching the first satellites. After Soviet satellites went up in 1957 and 1958, the US started Project Mercury to put men in orbit, while the Soviets secretly worked toward the same goal with their Vostok program. On 12 April 1961, Yuri Gagarin rode Vostok 1 around Earth once, becoming the first human in space. Alan Shepard followed on 5 May 1961 as the first American in space, on a suborbital flight aboard Freedom 7.

paragraphs.heading: Early firsts
paragraphs.text: In February 1962, John Glenn became the first American to orbit Earth. In June 1963 the Soviets launched Valentina Tereshkova, the first woman in space. The US then flew Project Gemini, ten missions with two-man crews in 1965 and 1966, to build the skills a Moon trip would need. Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk in March 1965 on the Soviet Voskhod 2. Gemini crews went on to make several spacewalks, stay in space for two weeks, and carry out the first rendezvous and docking of two spacecraft.

paragraphs.heading: To the Moon
paragraphs.text: The US built the Saturn V rocket to send Apollo spacecraft to the Moon, and in December 1968 Apollo 8 carried Frank Borman, James Lovell and William Anders around the Moon ten times. In July 1969, Apollo 11 landed Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin on the Moon and brought them home safely, along with command module pilot Michael Collins. By 1972, six Apollo missions had put 12 men on the lunar surface. The Apollo 13 crew survived a spacecraft failure, swung past the Moon without landing, and made it back to Earth safely.

paragraphs.heading: Stations and shuttles
paragraphs.text: The Soviet Union failed to develop the N1 rocket it needed to land people on the Moon, and it ended its lunar programs in 1974. It turned to space stations instead, using its three-person Soyuz craft to ferry cosmonauts up and back, starting with the Salyut stations from 1971 to 1986. In the US, a planning group proposed a large system built around a reusable Space Shuttle. President Nixon, judging that Congress would not fund such ambition, dropped every part except the Shuttle.

paragraphs.heading: Where things stand
paragraphs.text: People have been living in space without a break on the International Space Station since 2 November 2000. Since the last Moon landing in 1972, the only human trip beyond low Earth orbit has been the Artemis II flyby of the Moon in April 2026, and the US Artemis program aims to land on the Moon again in the late 2020s. Today only three countries, the US, Russia and China, have programs able to fly people. Private companies have built their own as well: SpaceShipOne made the first private launch with a person aboard in June 2004, and in May 2020 SpaceX made the first commercial launch of a crew into orbit, carrying NASA astronauts to the ISS.
